lesson.title: One Sender, One Receiver: Unicast as the Internet's Default Mode
lesson.summary: Unicast delivers a packet from exactly one sender to exactly one specific destination identified by its own unique IP address, and it is the delivery pattern behind the overwhelming majority of everyday internet traffic.
lesson.body:
At the network layer, every packet needs a destination, and the simplest possible arrangement is to address it to exactly one recipient. Unicast is precisely this: one sender, one receiver, with the packet's destination field carrying that single receiver's unique IP address. Every router along the path examines that destination address and forwards the packet one hop closer to it, using nothing more exotic than a routing table and a lookup, the same core network layer forwarding logic that handles all IP traffic regardless of what higher-layer protocol or application generated the packet.

Unicast depends directly on the idea of an IP address as a unique identifier. If two different hosts could share the same address, a router would have no way to know which one a unicast packet was actually meant for, since the entire delivery model rests on that address picking out one, and only one, destination. This is different from grouping many recipients under a shared address, which is what the following sections on multicast and broadcast will describe. Unicast is the default because most communication genuinely is one-to-one: a laptop loading a specific webpage from a specific server, an email client fetching messages from a specific mail server, or a phone opening a remote login session to a specific machine.

Consider a concrete case. A student opens a browser and requests a page from a university's course website. The browser's operating system already knows the server's IP address, resolved earlier through DNS, itself a stateless protocol relying on unicast queries and responses. The browser places that address in the destination field of its IP packets and sends them out. Each router between the student's laptop and the university's server looks only at that one destination address, consults its routing table, and forwards the packet toward it, typically using longest prefix matching to pick the most specific matching route. No other host on the path, not the student's roommate on the same Wi-Fi network, not another server the packet happens to route near, ever receives a copy. The reply from the university server comes back the same way, addressed unicast to the student's laptop alone.

Because unicast is a one-to-one relationship, it does not scale efficiently when the same content needs to reach many recipients at once. Streaming an identical video to ten thousand simultaneous viewers via unicast means generating ten thousand separate copies of that stream, one per destination address, even though the content is identical. That inefficiency is exactly the gap that multicast, broadcast, and anycast are each designed to close in different ways, each covered next.

It is worth noting that most large-scale video streaming today, services like Netflix or YouTube, still relies on unicast rather than true multicast, despite reaching enormous simultaneous audiences. Each viewer's device opens its own individual unicast connection to a nearby content delivery server, because true multicast delivery across the open internet was never widely deployed end to end between competing internet service providers. The illusion of one-to-many delivery at that scale is achieved by placing many unicast-serving copies close to viewers, not by the network layer replicating a single stream the way multicast does within a single administrative network.
